chapter: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
title: Ellington's clashes and Willie Smith's seating in the saxophone section
summary: Jones explains that Ellington's harsh writing would unnerve him and that Willie Smith disliked being seated apart from the saxes.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I was just about to ask you what would Ellington's music do to your nerves.
Well, the -- oh, the things with Johnny Hodges, the ballads, with Otto Hardwick, they're soothing. But when Ellington would start writing all those clashes, then
I'd have a breakdown and go right back in the operating room, I guess. I don't know.
You have to be pretty strong to go through that.

Because I remember Willy Smith, when he took Johnny Hodges' place in the Ellington band, and Duke had this setup where it was like a pyramid. Well, you know how he used to set up when -- I think Sonny -- no, Louis Bellson was with him. And Willy Smith would be way off to the left or off to the right, instead of sitting in with the reed section, like you normally see a band, you know?
So you can communicate with the other saxophone players. And Willy used to day, "Man, I don't know what I'm playing."
Because that's the way Duke did it. But out front it was beautiful. But the poor musician, sitting up there playing, he doesn't know who to blend with or what.
